paras: The lynching of John Taylor took place before dawn on June 12, 1881, when a large party of men took Taylor, a young Black farm hand, from the Greensboro, North Carolina, jail and hanged him by a road about seven miles from Reidsville in Rockingham County. Taylor and George Gunn had been accused of assaulting the wife of Col. James Irwin on June 3, and an attempt to lynch them at the Wentworth jail on June 5 had failed. North Carolina papers largely endorsed the killing, and a Danville wire carried it nationally as a lynching done during an eclipse of the moon.

According to the Charlotte Democrat, Taylor and Gunn worked for Irwin near Reidsville and on the night of June 3, while he and his daughter were in town, went to the house where Mrs. Irwin was alone with her young son. The papers said the men had meant to attack the daughter and assaulted the mother instead; one paper named them "Jim Taylor and Bob Green." Arrested the next day, they were reported to have confessed before a justice at Reidsville while a crowd talked of lynching, and were committed to the Wentworth jail. Taylor, aged 22, later blamed Gunn for the assault but admitted they had planned it together.

Warned on June 5 that a party would come for the prisoners that night, Sheriff Johnston of Rockingham left with Taylor by a roundabout route toward Kernersville. That night men forced the Wentworth jail doors after the jailer refused the keys, then, finding Taylor gone, left Gunn unharmed and rode after the sheriff. Taylor was lodged in the Greensboro jail, and when an armed party was expected there on June 6 the Guilford sheriff hid him outside town overnight.

Around 11 p.m. on Saturday, June 11, during the eclipse, a body of men rode into Greensboro and demanded the keys from the jailer, O. C. Wheeler. When he refused, they cut through three locked doors with sledges and chisels, freed Taylor from the chain holding him to the floor, and tied him to a waiting buggy. Estimates of the party ran from 50 or 60 horsemen to over 200 men, some described as masked or disguised, and a News and Observer correspondent wrote that women waved handkerchiefs as they left.

About 4 a.m., some seven miles from Reidsville, they set Taylor on the horse he was said to have ridden to the Irwin house and hanged him from a roadside oak. Large crowds, white and Black, came to see the body.

That evening a coroner's jury found that Taylor had been hanged "by unknown parties," and a Black man, Jupe Billard, buried him at the foot of the tree for $4 paid by the county. No arrest of any lyncher appears in the coverage, and Gunn, about whose guilt the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic saw "some doubt," was left in jail for a regular trial of which no report was found. The Charlotte Democrat asserted, without naming a source, that local Black residents thought Taylor "got his just deserts."

North Carolina papers mostly approved of the lynching. Even before it, the Western Sentinel wrote that "the courts should not be bothered" with the accused, and the Farmer and Mechanic regretted that the "lessons taught by the Ku Klux in 1871" were forgotten. Afterward the Farmer and Mechanic headlined "Dead and Done For! Decently and in Order!" and the Charlotte Democrat "Speedy Punishment," while the Greensboro Battle Ground alone said it regretted the occurrence and preferred that the law take its course.

Outside the state, a Danville dispatch of June 12 ran within two days from Maine and Minnesota to Texas under headlines such as "A Double Eclipse," and its dateline led some editors to place the lynching in Virginia. These wire items called Taylor "a negro" who had assaulted a white woman, stating the accusation as fact.

A Reidsville dispatch of June 15 put the seizure on "Monday night" with about sixty masked men, but dispatches dated June 12 support the Saturday date. The hanging site was given as seven miles south or southwest of Reidsville, or five miles away on the Greensboro road.

bases: A party of 50 to 200 men broke into the Greensboro jail, took John Taylor, held on an assault charge, and hanged him by the road near Reidsville, after an earlier party forced the Wentworth jail to reach him (A3, A10, A15, A18).

Taylor was taken by force from the Greensboro jail over the jailer's refusal and hanged by a party numbered at 50 to over 200 men, acting on the accusation that he had assaulted Mrs. Irwin; a coroner's jury found he was hanged by unknown parties (A10, A15, A17, A18).

A Greensboro dispatch, a Danville wire, the Greensboro Battle Ground, a News and Observer correspondent and the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic independently report the jail break and hanging (A9, A10, A15, A17, A18).

accounts.label: Greensboro Battle Ground
accounts.gist: Men from a rendezvous north of Greensboro cut through three jail doors, took Taylor at 11:30 p.m., and left for Reidsville in military order; over 200 in the body, thought to be Rockingham men.

accounts.label: Danville / Greensboro wire
accounts.gist: About 200 men broke open the jail during the eclipse and hanged Taylor seven miles south of Reidsville; the affair was done so quietly Greensboro learned of it afterward.

accounts.label: News and Observer correspondent
accounts.gist: Fifty or sixty men hanged Taylor from an oak at 4 a.m.; crowds viewed the body; coroner's jury found death by unknown parties.

accounts.label: Reidsville June 15 dispatch
accounts.gist: About sixty masked men entered Greensboro on 'Monday night'; the body hung near the Troublesome old ironworks, seven miles south-west of Reidsville.

accounts.label: Taylor's own statement
accounts.gist: Interviewed in Greensboro jail, Taylor said Gunn committed the assault while he stayed back, though he admitted they planned it together.

framing.detail: Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic: before the killing lamented forgotten 'lessons taught by the Ku Klux'; after it, 'Dead and Done For! Decently and in Order!' and 'no regrets'.
Western Sentinel: 'The courts should not be bothered with her outragers'; later 'Taylor, the Negro Rape Fiend Lynched... Speedy Retribution'.
Charlotte Democrat headed it 'Speedy Punishment' and reprinted the Greensboro North State's view that it was well deserved.
Greensboro Battle Ground regretted the occurrence and preferred the law take its course but said the men would not be blamed much.
Northern and western dailies ran the Danville wire under eclipse headlines ('A Double Eclipse', 'to Lynch a Bad Negro').
